# Combining Ag(II) and Ag(I) Reactivity Enables Electrophotochemical Acyl Fluoride Installation on (Hetero)Arenes

**Authors:** Elaine Reichert Raguram; Brandon M. Campbell; Jesse B. Gordon; Daniel G. Nocera

**Affiliations:** Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, 1812Harvard University, 12 Oxford Street, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138, United States

## Abstract

Merging the oxidative prowess of Ag­(II) with the Lewis acidity and halophilicity of Ag­(I) provides access to reactivity modes orthogonal to previously reported Ag­(II) electrophotocatalytic schemes. Herein, we demonstrate that the dual reactivity of Ag across its accessible oxidation states facilitates the direct fluorocarbonylation of arenes. First, CF2X radicals (X = Cl, Br) are generated via photoinduced ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) of Ag­(II) carboxylates in an undivided electrochemical cell. Ag­(II) turnover is sustained by utilizing stoichiometric Ag­(I), which undergoes electrochemical disproportionation into the active Ag­(II) photocatalyst and Ag(0). Second, the presence of excess Ag­(I) leads to in situ formation of synthetically valuable acyl fluorides from aryl–CF2X radical addition products through a halide abstraction process, enabling the direct conversion of aryl–H to aryl–COF. Mechanistic studies indicate that acyl fluorides form either via an SN1-like pathway featuring the intermediacy of a rare difluoro-carbocation, which was trapped and characterized crystallographically, or via SN2-like, Ag­(I)-assisted nucleophilic displacement of X by the carboxylate, depending on the electronic properties of the arene. With reaction conditions tailored to the electronic nature of each arene, acyl fluorides were synthesized directly from electronically diverse (hetero)­arene precursors. Furthermore, the reaction conditions developed for acyl fluoride synthesis may be extended to the perfluoroalkylation (X = F, CF3, CF2CF3) of a broad range of (hetero)­arenes in moderate-to-excellent yields. The reaction is tolerant of air and wet solvents, no supporting electrolyte is required, and the deposited Ag(0) can be quantitatively recovered as the AgNO3 precatalyst to maintain Ag atom economy.

## Introduction

The incorporation of carbon–fluorine (C–F) bonds into small-molecule therapeutics can dramatically improve their pharmacokinetic properties. Accordingly, approximately 20% of all pharmaceuticals contain fluorine, with aryl–fluoroalkyl linkages serving as particularly common motifs. The functionalization of arenes with fluoroalkyl groups can be efficiently accomplished by direct reaction with fluoroalkyl radical sources. Moving away from commonly employed fluoroalkyl radical donors, which tend to be expensive or not commercially available for fluoroalkyl groups beyond CF3, recently developed methods have sought to utilize abundant, inexpensive fluoroalkyl carboxylates as fluoroalkyl radical sources. However, many of these methods require forcing conditions − or stoichiometric carboxylate prefunctionalization. −

As an alternative strategy, ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) can provide access to the extreme redox potentials needed to furnish radicals directly from fluoroalkyl carboxylates under overall mild conditions with Fe complexes, − or as we have reported, , with Ag­(II) bipyridine complexes. For the latter, fluoroalkyl radical generation is enabled by electrophotocatalysis, which has emerged in recent years as a powerful platform for organic synthesis (Figure A, left). , In Ag­(II) electrophotocatalytic schemes, the role of Ag­(I) is relegated to simply serving as a precursor for Ag­(II). Inspired by redox-neutral photoredox schemes in which the reduced/oxidized photocatalyst following photoinduced single-electron transfer (SET) serves a pivotal role in further ground-state reactivity, we questioned whether Ag­(I) may serve an additional purpose, thus opening access to novel reactivity pathways (Figure A, right). While the exclusive role of Ag­(II) is as a single-electron oxidant, Ag­(I) exhibits additional reactivity modes, such as C–H activation, , due to its Lewis acidity and halophilicity. We envisioned that coupling the dual reactivity of Ag­(I) with Ag­(II) electrophotocatalytic cycles could provide access to alternative reactivity beyond fluoroalkylation. Namely, we posited that chloro- and bromodifluoromethyl carboxylates could be repurposed as latent acyl fluoride synthons upon Ag­(I) activation of the aryl–CF2X (X = Cl, Br) product generated via Ag­(II)-mediated decarboxylation (Figure B).

*1: (A) Reaction design principle: merging Ag­(II) electrophotocatalytic cycles with Ag­(I) ground-state reactivity has the potential to open new reactivity paradigms. (B) Ag­(I)-mediated halide activation may transform halodifluorocarboxylates into acyl fluoride synthons via nucleophilic attack of the intermediate aryl–CF2X with O-nucleophiles. (C) This work: direct conversion of aryl–H to aryl–COF or aryl–CF2X enabled by the unique reactivity of Ag across its accessible oxidation states.*

Acyl fluorides are highly desirable synthetic intermediates. Unlike structurally similar acyl chlorides, acyl fluorides are less prone to hydrolysis and are often stable to column chromatography. Accordingly, acyl fluorides can serve as useful intermediates for challenging acyl transfers, including peptide coupling, and they readily undergo oxidative addition into the C–F bond to participate in transition-metal-catalyzed cross-coupling reactions. , Given their broad synthetic utility, a general method for the conversion of aryl–H to aryl–COF is highly desirable. However, acyl fluorides are most often synthesized from the corresponding carboxylic acids, and few methods have been reported for the direct fluorocarbonylation of arenes. ,

Herein, we report that Ag­(II)-mediated photochemical decarboxylation of chloro- and bromodifluoromethyl carboxylates, coupled with the use of excess Ag­(I), leads to the direct installation of acyl fluorides onto a variety of (hetero)­arenes (Figure C). Mechanistic studies reveal acyl fluoride installation along two pathways, depending on the electronic nature of the substrate. Furthermore, the conditions employed for acyl fluoride synthesis enabled the perfluoroalkylation of arenes in an undivided electrochemical cell. Whereas superstoichiometric Ag­(I) is employed, the excess Ag may be quantitatively recovered and subsequently reused with no loss in reaction efficiency.

## Results and Discussion

### Undivided Electrochemical Cell Methodology

Our previous work utilized catalytic Ag (2.5 mol %) in a divided electrochemical cell to accomplish the electrophotocatalytic CF2X functionalization of arenes (X = F, CF3, CF2CF3, Cl, Br, CH3). , We suspected that a higher loading of Ag­(I) could result in the in situ reaction of aryl–CF2X (X = Cl, Br) products via activation of the halide by Ag­(I) (Figure B). Despite the high energy barriers expected for SN1- or SN2-like reactivity at a difluoromethylene unit, we envisioned that the highly halophilic nature of Ag­(I) could effectively mediate the transformation. Following nucleophilic attack, we expected that oxygen-based nucleophiles, such as the carboxylate or adventitious water, would collapse to form an acyl fluoride product due to the driving force associated with energetically favorable fluoride elimination and carbonyl formation.

With these principles in mind, an experimental setup was designed to employ excess Ag­(I) salts in an undivided electrochemical cell for several reasons. First, this setup ensures an ample concentration of Ag­(I) for in situ activation of aryl–CF2X species. Second, in combination with catalytic loadings of bpy, Ag­(I) should undergo electrochemical disproportionation, ensuring a steady supply of Ag­(II) for photochemical decarboxylations. Importantly, Ag(0) deposition at the cathode pins the cathodic potential to the favorable Ag­(I/0) couple, thus ensuring a minimized full-cell potential. Lastly, in addition to low cell potentials, undivided electrochemical cells offer a number of advantages as compared to their divided counterparts, including operational simplicity and decreased solution resistance. In particular, a lowered cell resistance could obviate the need for exogenous supporting electrolyte. Most reported organic electrochemical reactions require supporting electrolytes, presenting a significant challenge for the field as these electrolytes, particularly commonly employed tetrabutylammonium salts, can be difficult to purify from the organic products. The ability to circumvent supporting electrolyte thus facilitates product isolation and minimizes waste. Whereas the use of superstoichiometric Ag­(I) is a limitation, the deposited Ag(0) may easily be recovered as AgNO3 upon dissolution and crystallization from nitric acid (HNO3), effectively rendering HNO3 as the terminal oxidant.

The feasibility of the undivided electrochemical setup was first investigated using the trifluoromethylation of benzene as a model reaction. Utilizing AgNO3 (3 equiv), reticulated vitreous carbon (RVC) electrodes, and sodium trifluoroacetate as the CF3 source in a two-electrode undivided electrochemical cell under constant current conditions and blue light irradiation, 85% yield of trifluoromethylated products was observed (see Section S2.2 for full optimization details). Notably, these reaction conditions (1) are tolerant of water and air, (2) require no supporting electrolyte, and (3) facilitate product formation with yields exceeding those of the previously developed divided cell conditions. , The full-cell potential with constant current at 7.5 mA was ca. 1.3–1.6 V (Figure S2), whereas related fluoroalkylation methods using fluoroalkyl carboxylates require full-cell potentials of 2.8–3.5 V in direct Kolbe-type anodic oxidations or 2–2.5 V in Fe-mediated electrophotocatalytic schemes. , Moreover, the deposited Ag(0) could be quantitatively recovered (98%) by immersing the Ag-plated cathode in HNO3 to regenerate the AgNO3 precatalyst (see Section S7). Recognizing these substantial improvements upon our previously reported methodology, , the scope of (hetero)­arene perfluoroalkylation was eventually explored (vide infra); however, the immediate focus remained coupling Ag­(II) photochemical decarboxylation with Ag­(I) ground state reactivity.

### Acyl Fluoride Synthesis and Mechanism

The conditions of an undivided electrochemical cell allow for the spontaneous reaction of the intermediate aryl–CF2X (X = Cl, Br) with Ag­(I). The electrolysis of mesitylene and sodium chlorodifluoroacetate resulted in two distinct products in addition to the expected CF2Cl-functionalized products 2e and bis-2e (Table ). Isolation of these products (see Section S6.4) confirmed their identities as acyl fluorides 4b and 4b′. Subsequent investigation revealed a negative correlation between applied current and 4b formation (Entries 2 and 3). Presumably, increased current leads to rapid consumption of Ag­(I), decreasing its ability to react with generated 2e. Decreased carboxylate equivalents appeared to be beneficial for acyl fluoride formation (Entries 4 and 5); increased Ag equivalents (Entry 6) and increased concentration (Entries 7 and 8) also shifted the product distribution toward acyl fluoride formation. Recognizing that the significantly weaker C–Br bond strength compared to C–Cl could enable more efficient acyl fluoride formation, analogous experiments were performed with sodium bromodifluoroacetate (see Section S2.3). Here, 51% of 4b was formed with 5 equiv of the carboxylate and 3 equiv of Ag; however, 4b formation was accompanied by 35% yield of brominated mesitylene. With direct aryl–H to aryl–COF conversion demonstrated, we sought to delineate the reaction mechanism in order to understand the scope of the current methodology.

Initial insight into the reaction mechanism of fluorocarbonylation was sought using 1,3-dimethyluracil as a substrate, as the intermediate chlorodifluoromethylated product 2x is a nonvolatile solid and therefore readily isolable. We began by confirming that increased Ag­(I) concentration, as opposed to cathode-induced processes, is the primary factor leading to acyl fluoride formation in the undivided cell. In a divided cell with catalytic Ag loading (2.5 mol % Ag), no acyl fluoride is observed, and 2x is formed exclusively (Figure A). However, when excess Ag­(I) (3 equiv Ag) is added to a divided cell under otherwise identical conditions, the product distribution shifts entirely to acyl fluoride 4a, matching the product distribution observed under the undivided electrochemical conditions and thus confirming that Ag facilitates acyl fluoride formation. Furthermore, substantial amounts of 4a were formed under the strictly anhydrous conditions of a glovebox, implicating the carboxylate as the O-atom source (Figure A) as opposed to adventitious water. To definitively establish that both Ag­(I) and carboxylate are necessary for acyl fluoride formation, we subjected 2x to Ag­(I) and carboxylate, both separately and together (Figure B). Acyl fluoride 4a did not form in the absence of either Ag­(I) or carboxylate, suggesting that Ag­(I) is needed to activate Cl as a leaving group prior to nucleophilic attack by the carboxylate. −

To interrogate the mechanism of carboxylate substitution, we monitored the reaction of 2x with Ag­(I) in the absence of carboxylate (Figure B). Quantitative conversion of 2x to an intermediate that exhibited a dramatically deshielded aromatic 1H NMR signal (δ = 9.2 ppm, Figure S8) signified the presence of a strongly electron-withdrawing group, such as nitrilium (5a, Figure C), which could form via a Ritter-type mechanism involving nucleophilic attack by the CH3CN solvent at a difluoro-carbocation. In accordance with such an intermediate, X-ray crystallography reveals the production of a stable 4,4-difluoro-1,3-oxazine (6a), i.e., the cyclized species resulting from attack on the electrophilic carbon of 5a by the appropriately poised O atom nearby. To further probe the reactivity of the proposed nitrilium, 2x was exposed to Ag­(I) in t-BuCN as the solvent, resulting in the analogous 6b, in which t-BuCN is incorporated into the cyclized scaffold. Notably, oxazines 6a and 6b could be isolated on milligram scales, allowing for their complete characterization (see Section S4), including X-ray structures. The imidate carbon atom derived from either the CH3CN or t-BuCN solvent in 6a and 6b, respectively, is greatly distorted away from an idealized C­(sp2) geometry, suggesting high electrophilicity at this position (Figures S11 and S12). Indeed, under ambient conditions, 6a and 6b hydrolyze to 7a and 7b, respectively.

Acyl fluorides formed much less readily from more electron-deficient arenes. Slow formation of benzoyl fluoride (4j) from PhCF2Br (2y) was observed in the presence of Ag­(I) and NaO2CCF2Br, whereas the formation of 4j from PhCF2Cl (2b) was not observed (see Section S3.5). Whereas a weaker C–Br bond may promote more facile displacement of Br by the carboxylate compared to Cl, we also sought to determine whether the conversion of 2y to 4j proceeded via a carbocationic intermediate despite the absence of an electron-rich arene. Similar to the conversion of 2x to 4a (Figure B), 4j forms from 2y only in the presence of both Ag­(I) and carboxylate (see Section S3.5). Subjected to AgOTf in the absence of carboxylate, 2y decomposed and the formation of PhCF2OTf (8) was observed at early time points (Figure D). With the non-nucleophilic Ag­(I) counterion [B­(C6F5)4]−, 2y decomposed with a significantly slower rate, suggesting that while the difluoro-carbocation can form adjacent to a more electron-deficient arene, its formation is generally outcompeted by nucleophilic displacement.

Kinetics experiments were performed to interrogate the mechanistic differences of acyl fluoride formation for electron-rich vs electron-neutral arenes (see Section S5 for full details). We suspected that the conversion of 2x to 4a proceeded via an SN1-like mechanism due to the definitive crystallographic confirmation of nitrilium formation in the absence of carboxylate (6a). In support of this contention, initial rate kinetics revealed a first-order dependence on AgOTf and a zero-order dependence on the carboxylate nucleophile (Figure A). Conversely, we suspected that the conversion of 2y to 4j proceeds primarily via an SN2-like mechanism involving nucleophilic displacement of AgX, given our observation of PhCF2OTf (Figure D). Initial-rate kinetics revealed a second-order dependence of this reaction on AgOTf (Figure B), which is likely a convolution of two first-order dependencies on Ag­(I) and the triflate anion. To deconvolute these two kinetic dependencies, we performed additional experiments utilizing a Ag­(I) salt with the non-nucleophilic counterion [B­(C6F5)4]−. In the absence of carboxylate, first-order dependencies on AgB­(C6F5)4 (Figure B) and n-Bu4NOTf (Figure S21) were separately observed. Furthermore, a fractional (∼0.3) order dependence on the carboxylate was observed (Figures S22 and S23).

A proposed mechanism for the formation of acyl fluorides from electron-rich and electron-neutral halodifluoroarenes is shown in Figure . An initial Ag­(II) electrophotocatalytic cycle generates chloro- or bromo-difluoromethyl radicals, which are captured by the arene substrate. Electron-rich halodifluoroarenes, such as 2x, are then activated by Ag­(I), generating a difluoro-carbocation upon departure of AgX (X = Cl, Br). Electron-neutral halodifluoroarenes, such as 2y, proceed primarily via nucleophilic displacement of AgBr. Because acyl fluoride formation is not observed from electron-neutral chlorodifluoromethylated arenes, we propose that the nucleophilic displacement mechanism is not accessible from aryl–CF2Cl.

*4: Proposed mechanism of acyl fluoride formation from electron-rich and electron-neutral arenes.*

Building on these mechanistic insights, we were able to access acyl fluorides directly from a variety of electronically diverse arene precursors (see Section S6), including medicinally relevant heteroarenes, − by tailoring the reaction conditions to the electronic nature of each arene. Table divides the arene substrates into classes (I–IV) based on their reactivity: Class I arenes (4a–d) formed a mixture of aryl–CF2Cl and acyl fluoride with NaO2CCF2Cl as the carboxylate. Class II arenes (4e–f) exclusively formed the acyl fluoride with NaO2CCF2Cl, while Class III arenes (4g–h) formed exclusively aryl–CF2Cl. Both Class I and Class III arenes formed a mixture of acyl fluoride and aryl–Br with NaO2CCF2Br. The formation of aryl–Br side product for electron-rich arenes indicates the formation of Br radicals under the reaction conditions, likely via oxidation of Br– at the anode. Because an analogous phenomenon did not occur to such an extent for reactions with NaO2CCF2Cl, higher yields of acyl fluorides can be obtained from strongly electron-rich arenes by employing NaO2CCF2Cl as the carboxylate. Previously, the direct fluorocarbonylation of arenes was limited to electron-rich substrates, , but the strongly halophilic character of Ag­(I) promotes the formation of acyl fluorides from electron-neutral (4i–j) and electron-deficient Class IV arenes (4k–l); these substrates formed a mixture of acyl fluoride and aryl–CF2Br with NaO2CCF2Br. Particularly noteworthy is the synthesis of even a small amount of acyl fluoride 4l from the highly electron-deficient 1,4-difluorobenzene (3l), which is additionally polarity-mismatched with the electrophilic CF2Br radical.

*2 Fluorocarbonylation of Arenes*

### Extension to Perfluoroalkylations

We further sought to explore the scope of perfluoroalkylations in the undivided electrochemical cell given its success with the trifluoromethylation of benzene (vide supra). Optimized Ag­(II)-mediated conditions promoted efficient electrophotochemical fluoroalkylation of a broad scope of arene substrates, including pharmaceutically relevant heteroarenes and other drug-like substrates, with a variety of CF2X carboxylates (Table ). The formation of regioisomers or difunctionalized products from several substrates is consistent with the inherent reactivity of radical reactions. Reaction yields ranged from moderate to excellent, depending on the intrinsic reactivity of each arene substrate toward fluoroalkyl radical addition. , A wide range of medicinally prevalent heteroarenes − were functionalized effectively. Substrates containing potentially reactive functional groups, including benzylic protons (2c, 2e–g), aryl halides (2d, 2h, 2u), and N–H heterocycles (2j–l, 2v–w), were also well tolerated. Product 2v was synthesized using recovered AgNO3 with no loss of efficiency. We further established the utility of the undivided reaction setup by fluoroalkylating several structurally complex natural products and drug-like substrates (2m–w). Among these complex arenes, the undivided setup enabled the functionalization of substrates that did not perform well in our previously reported divided cell. Caffeine (2s–t), a moderately electron-rich arene, is oxidized by the active [Ag­(bpy)2]2+ complex in the ground state. In the divided cell, caffeine is likely oxidized at the anode, resulting in low yields (Supporting Information, p S57). Yet under these undivided conditions, caffeine is converted to fluoroalkylated products in good yields.

*3 Photoelectrochemical Perfluoroalkylation of Arenes*

Notably, our mechanistic studies of acyl fluoride formation indicated that Class III and IV arenes (vide supra) can readily form chlorodifluoromethylated products under the undivided reaction conditions. Thus, these products may be obtained in moderate-to-high yields for both simple arenes (2b–2d) and heteroarenes (2g, 2i), as well as medicinally relevant substrates (2q, 2t, 2w). The formation of product 2e could be favored over the corresponding acyl fluoride by employing decreased reaction concentration and increased current, as demonstrated in Table .

## Conclusion

In summary, we have elucidated a previously unexplored mechanism for the synthesis of acyl fluorides directly from unfunctionalized arene substrates. Central to this mechanism is the combined reactivity of Ag across its accessible oxidation states: Ag­(II) electrophotocatalytic cycles oxidize fluoroalkyl carboxylates via LMCT for aryl–CF2X (X = Cl, Br) generation, and excess Ag­(I) further activates these intermediates to produce acyl fluorides. The halophilicity of Ag­(I) promotes halide abstraction through either unstable difluoro-carbocations or nucleophilic displacements at difluoromethylene units, depending on the electronic character of the arene. We anticipate that the diverse reactivity of Ag­(I) can be more generally integrated with the broad potential of Ag­(II) LMCT activation of other redox-reticent substrates, informing the development of electrophotochemical methodologies with novel reaction pathways.
